Mihir Sharma

When a blind person asks a visual assistant whether a food carton has expired, a confident but wrong answer is more than a model error. It can shape a decision that is hard to verify independently. I’m Mihir Sharma, an independent HCI researcher working on haptic and wearable interfaces and human-AI interaction. I study how AI systems can communicate what they perceive, what they do not know and when they may be wrong through touch and other nonvisual channels, and whether these signals help people judge when to rely on AI without giving up control of their decisions.

Currently, I am working on:

  • Can a Buzz Answer That?Which questions to a visual assistant could be answered by vibration instead of speech. ACM IUI 2027, under review
  • TrueTapKeeping a smartwatch’s false buzzes within a limit each wearer sets. PACM IMWUT, under review
  • Material ConfidenceWhich study outcome can show whether people use AI confidence they feel rather than see. ACM CHIIR 2027, under review
  • SenseShiftWhat a navigation assistant should tell blind and low-vision pedestrians, and when. Working paper
  • Feel the FrameTouch cues that help blind users recover from a failed photo, one correction at a time. Working paper

I received my MFA in User Experience Design, with Distinction, from the College for Creative Studies, Detroit, advised by Prof. Predrag K. Nikolić. My thesis, TactileGrip, which received the CCS Thesis Select Award and an Iron A’ Design Award, is a set of sensor-embedded climbing holds that signal an approaching hand with sound and confirm contact with vibration. I designed it from 20 interviews with blind and low-vision climbers, guides, coaches and gym staff. In a within-participant test, all ten blindfolded sighted expert climbers progressed farther with TactileGrip than with verbal guidance alone (exact sign test, p = .002).

I also hold a Bachelor’s in Product Design from the University of Petroleum and Energy Studies, India. My design work, including a General Motors–sponsored self-driving car concept, is further down this page. Design taught me to build things; research is how I find out why they work.

The questions that stayed with me

I started by designing physical objects. Over time, I became more interested in the information they communicate, and in what happens when the system behind that information begins making decisions of its own.

  1. 2016–2020

    Physical product design

    During my Bachelor’s in Product Design, I worked through sketches, CAD, ergonomic studies, material experiments and physical prototypes. I learned that an object communicates before anyone reads an instruction: its shape suggests where to grip, its resistance signals how to move, and its physical feedback confirms an action.

    The question I carried forward

    How much can someone understand through physical interaction alone?

  2. 2020–2025

    Digital interaction design

    Moving into digital interfaces changed the problem. When I worked on Vangard, a General Motors–sponsored autonomous-vehicle concept, I was designing how a system’s perception and intentions could become understandable to passengers.

    My MFA thesis, TactileGrip, brought that question back into the physical world. A climbing hold could sense an approaching hand, communicate proximity and confirm contact without requiring a screen. Building and evaluating it showed me that sensing something accurately and communicating it effectively are two different problems.

    The question I carried forward

    How should a system translate what it senses into feedback a person can immediately interpret?

  3. 2025–present

    HCI research

    As a material research assistant at Ecosphere Organics, I explored biodegradable materials embedded with sensing technologies. The work kept me close to physical computing, but my interest was shifting from what materials and devices could detect to what people should be told about it.

    In July 2025, alongside that work, I began independent research on tactile communication in human-AI interaction. The problem has several parts: determining which answers can be encoded through vibration (Can a Buzz Answer That?), controlling unnecessary interruptions (TrueTap), and understanding how people interpret communicated uncertainty (Material Confidence).

    The question I’m pursuing next

    How can tactile interfaces help blind and low-vision people decide what information from an AI assistant deserves their attention, and when to trust it?

    That is the research direction I want to pursue through a PhD, developing and evaluating these systems with blind and low-vision communities.

Under review 3 papers

PACM IMWUT Journal · submitted Nov 2026, under review

TrueTap: Budgeting How Often a Smartwatch Buzzes You by Mistake

Mihir Sharma

  • QuestionHow can a smartwatch keep its false buzzes within a limit each wearer chooses?
  • ContributionA calibration method that sets the activity detector’s threshold so that only a chosen share of wearers go over their false-buzz budget, with a finite-sample guarantee. Released as a Python library and a browser runtime.
  • EvidenceOn day-long wrist recordings from 151 adults (CAPTURE-24), 3.7% of wearers went over budget, within the 9.8% bound, against 7.6% with a fixed threshold, while recall went from 0.65 to 0.60. Tested on three more datasets; a rerun from the raw recordings reproduced all 97,920 result rows (212 checks).
  • LimitationThe guarantee holds only when new wearers resemble the calibration wearers. The method has not yet run on a watch or with users; an online study (N = 160) and a lab study (N = 36) are designed.

Submitted manuscript (PDF, anonymous review version)

ACM IUI 2027 Poster · submitted Oct 2026, under review

Can a Buzz Answer That? How Much of What Blind People Ask a Visual Assistant Fits a Vibration Vocabulary

Mihir Sharma

  • QuestionHow many of the questions blind people ask a visual assistant could be answered by vibration instead of speech?
  • ContributionA small vibration vocabulary for yes, no, numbers, colours, “can’t tell” and “unsure”; rules for when to buzz and when to speak; and Felt Answers, an offline phone prototype designed for a planned study with blind and low-vision participants.
  • EvidenceOf 8,000 held-out questions from blind people (VizWiz), 15.5% fit a rhythm and 26.8% more a felt “can’t tell”. A zero-shot vision-language model (ViLT) still buzzed an answer for 38% of 2,147 photos marked unanswerable, and only 32% of its confident buzzes were correct. One script rebuilds every number (49 checks).
  • LimitationNo one has felt the rhythms in a study yet, and touch was not reliably faster than speech.

Submitted manuscript (PDF)Poster (PDF)

ACM CHIIR 2027 Short Paper · submitted Oct 2026, under review

Material Confidence: Which Outcomes Can Tell Felt from Seen AI Confidence?

Mihir Sharma

  • QuestionIf an AI’s confidence is felt as a vibration instead of seen on a screen, which study outcome can show whether people use it?
  • ContributionA design analysis that picks the outcome before any data are collected, plus a study protocol ready for preregistration, a web study app and band firmware.
  • EvidenceA re-analysis of 35,670 human-AI decisions from 1,125 people (HAIID), then simulation. Under the modeled assumptions, in simulated 96-person studies, reliance sensitivity detected an informative confidence cue 99% of the time, against 7% for a conventional appropriate-reliance measure, which would need about 1,820 participants.
  • LimitationThe power results come from simulation and assume people read the vibration correctly 80% of the time. The study has not run, and no one has felt the patterns.

Submitted manuscript (PDF, anonymous review version)

Master’s thesis 2023–24

MFA Thesis College for Creative Studies, Sep 2023–May 2024

TactileGrip: Real-time Sensor-Embedded Climbing Holds for Non-Visual Route Navigation

Mihir Sharma · Thesis advisor: Predrag K. Nikolić

  • Iron A’ Design Award, 2026
  • Winner, Thesis Select Award, College for Creative Studies, 2024
  • Nominee, UX Design Awards, New Talent, Berlin, 2024
  • QuestionCan climbing holds guide the hand directly, giving blind and low-vision climbers more independence from a guide’s spoken directions?
  • ContributionWorking holds with one cue for each moment: a beep that quickens as the hand approaches, a vibration on grip, a hold shape that points to the next hold, and star-shaped holds that announce progress aloud. Built with an Arduino Nano, an ultrasonic sensor read every 50 ms, a vibration motor and 3D-printed forms.
  • EvidenceDesigned from 20 interviews with blind and low-vision climbers, guides, coaches and gym staff. In a within-participant test, all 10 blindfolded sighted expert climbers progressed farther with TactileGrip than with verbal guidance alone (exact sign test, p = .002), and their partners gave no hold-level directions.
  • LimitationBlindfolded sighted climbers cannot stand in for blind and low-vision climbers.

Led to SenseShift.

Working papers 2 manuscripts

Working paper Nov 2026

SenseShift: Adaptive AI‑to‑Haptic Communication

Mihir Sharma

  • QuestionWhat should a navigation assistant tell blind and low-vision pedestrians, and how can it do so without competing with the sounds they rely on?
  • ContributionAn interruption policy that predicts how close each object will come, and a vibration code for a six-pod forearm band. Python and browser versions make identical decisions on 5,753 test frames.
  • EvidenceOn 1,000 held-out simulated walks in the main suite, it warned of 90.0% of hazards one to five seconds ahead, with 8.7% of messages about distractors, against 71.3% and 63.7% for announcing the nearest object. The distractor share rose in the crowded and degraded-perception suites.
  • LimitationAll results are computational. The band is designed but not built, and three studies with blind and low-vision adults are designed but have not run.

Grew out of TactileGrip.

Working paper in preparation

Feel the Frame: Touch-Guided Camera Aiming for Blind Users of Visual AI Assistants

Mihir Sharma

  • QuestionWhen a photo fails, how can touch help a blind user take a better one before the assistant answers?
  • ContributionAn error-recovery policy: five photo-flaw detectors (too dark, overexposure, blur, obstruction, framing) drive one cue at a time through a four-motor sleeve, stay quiet for the shutter, and hand control back when a correction fails. A working web prototype runs the policy.
  • EvidenceEvaluated on 7,750 VizWiz photos, with half held out. Held-out AUROC ranged from .66 for framing to .95 for too dark.
  • LimitationAll results are computational. The sleeve is designed but not built, and no one has felt the cues yet.

Companion to Can a Buzz Answer That?: one helps take the photo, the other answers by touch.

What connects this work

These projects examine different decisions an assistive AI system must make before communicating through touch: which information can be encoded, which events deserve an interruption, how to help someone recover when the camera cannot see well enough, and how uncertainty should be represented and evaluated.

Next, I want to study how multimodal AI assistants can communicate uncertainty in ways people can act on: when to say that perception is uncertain, when to ask for another input, and whether to use touch, speech or both while someone is busy with a demanding task. I plan to work through co-design with blind and low-vision participants, functional prototypes and controlled experiments, measuring error recognition, appropriate reliance, interruption burden and user agency alongside task completion.

Selected design work

Before studying how AI communicates through touch, I designed interactions for autonomous vehicles, immersive environments and agricultural tools. These projects shaped how I think about system behavior, human understanding and evaluation.

General Motors Sponsored studio, 2024

Vangard: Autonomous Mobility for Chongqing in 2040

Mihir Sharma (UX), with an exterior and an interior designer

Shortlisted by GM; one of two teams invited to refine it with GM designers over the summer

  • QuestionHow do passengers understand the intentions of a car that makes decisions on their behalf?
  • ContributionAs the team’s UX designer, I designed how the car communicates automation state, warnings and intent to passengers, and how they override it, across the HUD, cluster and center screen (45+ infotainment wireframes).
  • EvidenceA think-aloud test with 5 participants in a physical cabin mockup, across four task scenarios, changed three design decisions before the GM review.
  • LimitationA speculative concept for 2040; the test was small and formative, not a measured evaluation.

Ars Electronica Festival Linz, 2023

DetroTune: Motown Techno, Detroit’s Music History in VR

Mihir Sharma, Raghunath Rajasekar, Siddhi Sakhare, Mahsa Khoshkbar Foroushan, Sara Fallahi

Exhibited at Ars Electronica Festival and Detroit Month of Design

  • QuestionHow does a spatial-audio VR experience affect recall of cultural history, and engagement with it, compared with video?
  • ContributionMotown Techno, our team’s piece in the Detro Tune exhibition: a VR journey through Detroit’s downtown and its techno music. I designed the spatial experience and built it in Unity with 3D sound and motion feedback.
  • EvidenceA mixed-methods study with 40 participants compared the VR piece with video-based learning: recall was 32% higher and emotional engagement 28% higher with VR.
  • LimitationA team course project with one comparison condition (video).

Farmacy: AI for Agricultural Resilience

Mihir Sharma

  • QuestionHow can smallholder farmers with varied literacy levels access crop information, market prices and buyers through one interface?
  • ContributionA farming app for crop planning and equipment rental, with field mapping and profit forecasting. I did the field research, designed the workflow and designed the interface.
